question: We already work with an agency or medical education partner. How do you fit in?
answer: Easily, in our experience. We're not trying to replace your existing relationships. Most of our clients work with medical education companies, PR agencies or advertising partners alongside us, and we're used to operating as part of a broader ecosystem. We know where we add the most value: the creative and production work that requires deep cardiology knowledge, high production standards and genuine storytelling craft. If your medical education partner is handling the clinical content and your PR agency is handling the press, we're the people making sure the content itself is compelling enough to do the job it's been given.

question: Can you work across multiple languages and markets?
answer: Yes, and we've learned how to do it without it becoming the thing that kills the story. The temptation with multilingual projects is to shoot everything separately for every market, which multiplies cost and time and usually produces inconsistent results. We build for it from the start: a core creative that works across markets, with localisation built into the production process rather than bolted on afterwards. We've produced content with English, French, German, Italian and Spanish speakers, shot in the same creative framework, that feels coherent and intentional rather than translated. If you're working across European markets, or globally, we know how to make that work.

question: You're known for VR. Is that all you do?
answer:
VR is one of the things we do particularly well, and it tends to get attention at congresses, which is probably why it's what people notice first. But it's one format among many. We make documentary films, animation, live case recordings and broadcasts, as well as social content interactive digital experiences, and of course, the more standard (but often important) webinars - including live broadcasts.

What stays the same across all of it is the strategic thinking and the storytelling. The format is always in service of the story, never the other way around. If VR is the right tool for what you're trying to achieve, we'll recommend it. If it isn't, we'll tell you that too.

question: How do you work with KOLs?
answer: Carefully. KOLs are putting their clinical reputation on the line every time they appear on camera, and they know it. They're busy, they're precise, and they're protective of how they're represented. We've learned how to earn that trust: how to brief them properly, how to get the best performance, and how to make sure the final content reflects well on them as well as on you. Your KOL relationships take years to build. We treat them accordingly.

question: How do you handle compliance and medical review?
answer: We've been through it enough times to know how it works. Medical affairs, regulatory review, legal sign-off, multiple stakeholders with conflicting opinions: we build all of that into the process from the start, not as an afterthought. We arrive with an idea that can survive review without losing its impact. That's a craft in itself, and it's one we've spent years developing. The goal is always the same: content that's scientifically watertight and still compelling enough to change minds.

question: How are you different from a medical education company?
answer: Medical education companies are brilliant at the science. They know how to construct a clinically rigorous curriculum, get it past an advisory board and deliver it to the right accreditation standard. That's not what we do. We're a creative agency that happens to know cardiology very well. Our job is to make sure the science lands with the emotional force it deserves: that it's remembered, that it changes how someone thinks, that it moves them to act differently in the cath lab. The two things are complementary, which is why we often work alongside medical education partners rather than instead of them. They bring the clinical rigour. We make sure it's impossible to ignore.

question: How do we make the case for agency investment internally?
answer: We hear this a lot, and we take it seriously. The honest answer is that we help you make the case. Before we start any project, we're clear on what it's trying to achieve: a behaviour change, an adoption rate, a congress moment, a sales tool that actually gets used. That clarity makes it easier to demonstrate value after the fact. We can also point to a body of work with some of the most respected names in cardiology, including Abbott, Philips, Medtronic and Shockwave, which tends to help with internal conversations about whether we're a credible partner. And if it's useful, we're happy to talk to your budget holder directly about what we'd deliver and why it's worth it.

question: How do you make sure the science is right without killing the creativity?
answer: This is the tension at the heart of everything we do, and we've learned to embrace it rather than resolve it. The science has to be watertight. There's no version of this where we sacrifice accuracy for a better story. But accuracy and compelling aren't opposites. The best cardiology stories we've told have been the ones where the science itself was the drama: an accidental discovery in a laboratory, a device that shouldn't have worked but did, a clinician who saw something nobody else had seen. The science doesn't need to be simplified to be compelling. It needs to be told properly. Our job is to find the story that's already in the science, and tell it in a way that medical affairs can approve and a busy cardiologist won't forget.
